primary_text:
I've never said this out loud, not even to my accountant. I have three online stores built and sitting in the admin, and I haven't done anything with them in years.

I run a small clothing shop. The back room is where I do the books, at a desk wedged between two rails of stock and a box of spare hangers.

Every March my accountant sits in that room with me and goes through the year line by line. This year he stopped on the platform fees.

"What are these three?" he asked.

"My online stores," I said.

"How are they doing?"

"Slow," I said. Which was a lie. Slow would have meant something was happening.

The truth is they were built. Themes picked, pages set up, a few products half chosen. Ready to be loaded, and just sitting there. I had been paying every month for three stores nobody had visited in years.

He didn't push. He made a small pencil mark next to the line and moved on. I remember that mark more than anything else he said that day.

After he left I sat there with the laptop shut. It was 6:40. The shop was closed. I could hear the rail creak when the heating came on. I didn't open it.

I didn't know yet that the thing that changed it would be a stranger with a pen at the shipping counter.

Anyway. I should back up.

I bought this shop with most of what I had saved. It was supposed to be the steady part. The online side was supposed to be the growth.

For a few years the marketing was the one bringing in the money. Then it slowed down so much that some weeks the door barely opened.

The first store I built myself, over a winter of evenings. It went live in November. By the second week of December I was packing orders at midnight, sending them off late, and apologizing to people I had never met. I'm good at a lot of things, but I have very little time.

"I had one before," I would tell people later. "I just ended it because I was dealing with a lot."

The second store I built in a weekend, full of good intentions. It never had a single product loaded.

For the third, I did what everyone says to do. I asked about hiring someone.

I got three quotes. $5,000. $20,000. $15,000.

I'm like, seriously? Come on.

I would not pay $2,500 to anybody unless I could see some results. Let alone twenty thousand.

What I actually wanted was someone to fully automate my online business. I would have paid for that. Just not twenty thousand dollars of it, up front, on a promise.

So I built the third one myself too. Watched the videos, picked a theme, and it went live on a Sunday afternoon. Then Monday came, the shop needed me, and it sat.

I added it up once. Three stores. The monthly fees. A theme I paid for twice. The weekends I will never get back. I stopped adding.

Some nights I would open the admin, look at the three store names, and close it again without clicking anything. It felt like opening a drawer of bills.

What I told myself was always the same. I'm not a computer person. I don't have the time. I can't compete with the big stores anyway.

None of that turned out to be the reason.

The reason showed up on an ordinary Sunday, doing stock in the shop.

I was moving the scarves to the front because they had sold. I was marking down a jacket that hadn't moved in six weeks. I was changing the window. And somewhere between the price gun and the mannequin, I realized I had done this every single week for eleven years.

That's the job. Opening day isn't the job. The job is every week after it. See what sells, move it forward, take out what doesn't, bring in the next thing.

I would never open up once, flip the sign, and walk away for three years.

That is exactly what happened to all three of my stores.

That night I went looking for why. I found the platform's own guide for people who build stores for clients. It says the builder can "transfer ownership to the client when it's ready to go live."

Ready to go live. That is where the builder's job is designed to end.

Here is what I finally understood. On launch day a store is a set of guesses. Which products. Which photos. Which price. Which words in the title. The first weeks after it opens are when those guesses finally get tested by real people. Somebody clicks and leaves. One product gets looked at and nothing else does. A listing gets no attention at all.

That information is worth nothing unless somebody reads it and acts on it. Fix the listing. Drop the product nobody wants. Put the next one live. Test it small. Read it again.

Nobody was assigned to that work on my stores. Not the builder, whose job ended on launch day. Not me, because the shop takes the whole day. So each store froze on the day it went live and stayed exactly like that.

It wasn't the platform, and it wasn't me. A built store is not a running store, and nobody had the job of running mine.

Which raised a worse question. Who would take that job? I didn't have the hours, and the people who did wanted twenty thousand dollars.

I got my answer in a queue.

A few days later I was at the shipping counter with two returns. The woman ahead of me had a stack of small parcels, all labeled. Online orders.

I said something like, "I've got online stores too."

She turned around. "So who's working on them?"

I opened my mouth to answer and realized nobody ever had.

Her first store, she said, had been handed over the day it went live, and the builder disappeared. Then she took the pen from the counter, turned my receipt over, and drew two lines. A short one and a long one.

"Everyone quotes you this," she said, tapping the short one. Then the long one. "This is the part that decides it."

A small team built the store she has now, in her name, and they're still on it. Products go live in stages, small ad tests on a budget she approves, and a written review of what to keep and what to replace.

"It's not automatic," she said. "I approve the budget and read what they send. I just don't do the work."

She wrote a name under the two lines. Readymerce. Then she was gone.

I didn't trust it. I pay $500 and then I'm going to have to pay more money down the road, I thought.

So I read their page the way my accountant reads a receipt.

The $500 is one-time. The store is opened in your name and stays in your name. Products are picked from search demand and competition data and go live in stages, each with a small ad test on a budget you approve. After launch: an early performance review, corrections, new products.

Then the part most companies bury. Product costs, platform fees and ad spend are yours, not in the $500. The ongoing work is quoted on the call before you commit. No income guarantees. I trusted that more than a promise.

The refund I read twice. Seven days from payment, the $500 fee only, and it ends when you accept delivery, buy any add-on, or ask for more work.

On the call I said it straight. Show me exactly what the $500 pays for. They did, line by line, including after launch day. And they said it isn't fully automatic. I approve budgets and read reports. They do the work.

My own stores sat because the shop needed me. The agencies wanted $5,000 to $20,000 before I saw anything. A builder hands it over on launch day. This was $500, every other cost named, and the work after launch on the list.

"I'll start with the 500," I said.

It was a new store, built in my name, on the platform we agreed on the call. The first time I logged in, my own name was in the owner field. I looked at it longer than I'd like to admit.

Products went live in stages, the first test on a budget I approved. What to do next was no longer my job.

Then the first written review came in.

I opened it in the back room at 6:40, shop closed, the rail creaking. The laptop was open this time.

It said what to keep. What to replace, and why. Which listings they had already fixed, and what was going live next.

It was the first time in years anyone had done anything with a store of mine after launch day.

Relief, mostly. Like someone had finally walked into a room I had left the lights on in for three years.

The next March, my accountant stopped on the platform fees again. I told him the truth. Three stores that sat. One that's live, in my name, with a team still on it. He rubbed out his pencil mark.

If I could tell the owner I was that night at 6:40 one thing, it would be this. You didn't fail at building stores. You built three. Nobody ever had the job of working them after they went live.

Every month mine sat, I paid for stores that did nothing. The $500 Build is what I started with, in my name, in stages, on a budget I approve. And they stay after launch day.

The receipt with the two lines is still on my desk.

P.S. The build was never the hard part. Ask anyone you talk to the question she asked me: who's working on it after it goes live? Mine finally has someone. It's loaded and live.
